title-group.article-title: Fraction dose escalation of split-course concurrent chemoradiotherapy following induction chemo-immunotherapy in unresectable locally advanced oesophageal squamous carcinoma in China (GASTO-10102): a single-centre phase 1 study

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The optimal fractionation patterns and safety of hypofractionated radiotherapy remain poorly defined in locally advanced oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (LA-ESCC). We aimed to determine the maximum tolerated fraction dose (MTFD) of split-course concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) following induction chemo-immunotherapy in patients with LA-ESCC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this phase 1 study, patients (aged 18–80 years) with unresectable, histologically confirmed LA-ESCC (stage T1-4, N0-3, M0-1 disease; ECOG 0–1) were enrolled from one site in China (Sun yat-sen University Cancer Center, Guangzhou, Guangdong). Eligible participants had no prior treatment with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery, or immunotherapy for ESCC and no evidence of deep ulceration on baseline esophagoscopy. Enrolled participants received two cycles of induction albumin-bound paclitaxel (260 mg/m2, d1), cisplatin (60 mg/m2, d1), and toripalimab (240 mg, d1) every three weeks, followed by definitive split-course radiotherapy with oral capecitabine (1000 mg/m2, twice daily on days 1–14 of each radiotherapy course). Radiotherapy was delivered in two courses separated by a 4-week break using volumetric modulated arc therapy. Three dose levels were evaluated sequentially in cohorts of six patients: level 1 (30 Gy in 10 fractions + 20 Gy in 10 fractions), level 2 (28 Gy in 7 fractions + 22 Gy in 10 fractions), and level 3 (25 Gy in 5 fractions + 25 Gy in 10 fractions). The primary endpoint was MTFD within 12 months after completion of CCRT. The primary endpoint and safety analysis were assessed in all patients who received any study treatment. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06020885.

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: Between Aug 31, 2023, and July 23, 2024, 18 patients were enrolled (n = 6 per dose), and all completed split-course CCRT per protocol. The MTFD was not reached, and dose level 3 was tolerable. The most common grade 3 toxicity was lymphopenia (72.2%), followed by esophagitis (11.1%). No grade 4 or 5 toxicities occurred. The objective response rate after induction therapy was 100%. After CCRT, the clinical complete response rate was 83.3%. With a median follow-up of 20.5 months, median progression-free and overall survival were not reached; 1-year rates were 88.9% and 94.4%, respectively.

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: Fraction dose-escalated split-course CCRT following induction chemo-immunotherapy was feasible, well tolerated, and showed encouraging preliminary efficacy. Larger prospective studies are warranted.

sec.title: Evidence before this study
sec.p: Definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) is the standard treatment for unresectable locally advanced oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (LA-ESCC), but outcomes remain unsatisfactory. Several studies have suggested that induction chemo-immunotherapy before CCRT may improve tumour response. However, the tolerability, optimal fractionation patterns, and safety of hypofractionated or split-course radiotherapy delivered after induction chemo-immunotherapy remain poorly defined in oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma. To address this knowledge gap, we searched PubMed for clinical trials published in English between database inception and Jan 4, 2026, using the search terms (“locally advanced oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma” or “locally advanced oesophageal squamous cell cancer” or “locally advanced oesophageal cancer” or “oesophageal squamous cell cancer”), AND (“induction” or “neoadjuvant” or “chemo-immunotherapy”), AND (“chemoradiotherapy” or “chemoradiation” or “radiotherapy”), AND (“hypofractionation” or “fraction dose escalation”). No prospective phase 1 studies were identified that evaluated hypofractionated or fraction dose–escalated split-course CCRT following induction chemo-immunotherapy, and the maximum tolerated fraction dose (MTFD) in this setting remained unknown. We aimed to address this evidence gap.

sec.title: Added value of this study
sec.p: This prospective phase 1 study is the first to determine the MTFD of fraction dose–escalated split-course CCRT following induction chemo-immunotherapy in unresectable LA-ESCC. Three hypofractionated regimens were tested while maintaining a comparable biologically effective dose. No MTFD was reached at the highest planned dose level, and no grade 4–5 treatment-related toxicities were observed. The treatment was feasible and achieved a high clinical complete response rate after CCRT, with encouraging early progression-free and overall survival outcomes.

sec.title: Implications of all the available evidence
sec.p: Our preliminary findings suggest that radiotherapy fractionation can be safely intensified using a split-course, hypofractionated approach after effective systemic induction therapy. Defining tolerable fraction doses in this context provides a foundation for optimizing radiotherapy–immunotherapy integration and supports further evaluation in phase 2 and 3 trials.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a predominant global health challenge, particularly in Eastern Asia.1 For patients with unresectable locally advanced ESCC (LA-ESCC), definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) represents the standard of care.2 However, this approach is associated with substantial toxicity, including severe esophagitis, pneumonitis, and hematologic adverse events, which often lead to treatment interruptions and can compromise outcomes.3,4 For patients treated with standard-of-care CCRT, grade ≥3 esophagitis occurred in 7.0%–28.8%, and treatment-related death occurred in 3.3%–6.0%.5, 6, 7 Consequently, strategies to enhance the therapeutic ratio by improving efficacy while mitigating toxicity are urgently needed.

The integration of immunotherapy with chemotherapy has transformed the treatment paradigm for LA-ESCC. Induction chemo-immunotherapy offers a compelling strategy to cytoreduce tumours, potentially eradicate micro-metastatic disease, and induce a synergistic immunologic environment that may augment the effects of subsequent radiotherapy.8,9 Our preliminary study demonstrated an objective response rate of 93.4% to induction chemo-immunotherapy, indicating that substantial tumour burden reduction can be achieved prior to radiotherapy.10 This tumour shrinkage may facilitate the subsequent delivery of definitive CCRT with a reduced risk of treatment-related toxicities. Two recent phase 2 studies provide further support for integrating induction chemoimmunotherapy prior to CCRT in LA-ESCC, demonstrating encouraging survival and improved local control compared to historical data.11,12 Furthermore, advances in radiotherapy technology have revived interest in hypofractionation, allowing the delivery of higher biological doses per fraction with improved precision and safety. Hypofractionated radiotherapy (hypo-RT) may not only improve local tumour control through a higher biologically effective dose (BED) but could also potentiate the abscopal effect by promoting immunogenic cell death and enhancing antigen presentation.13,14

A critical limitation to dose escalation in oesophageal CCRT is the risk of severe cumulative toxicities, including fistula formation, massive bleeding, and injury to adjacent organs at risk such as the lungs, and heart.3,6 The rationale for hypofractionation in ESCC is supported by experience in rectal cancer, where short-course preoperative radiotherapy (25 Gy in 5 fractions) has demonstrated excellent tumour regression and minimal risk of perforation or bleeding, offering a valuable reference for radiotherapy in hollow visceral organs.15 However, evidence from prior studies indicates that continuous, whole-course hypo-RT is associated with significant treatment-related toxicities in patients with LA-ESCC.16 Building on our previous studies in non-small cell lung cancer, we adopted a split-course radiotherapy strategy, incorporating a planned mid-treatment break following the initial phase of hypo-RT.17,18 This approach allows normal tissue recovery and resolution of acute toxicities, thereby facilitating completion of a full-course radiotherapy regimen that might otherwise be intolerable if delivered continuously.

Building on this rationale, we hypothesised that a novel regimen combining induction chemo-immunotherapy to maximize systemic and local immune priming, followed by a fraction dose-escalated, split-course CCRT protocol with a planned break for recovery, would be both feasible and safe. This phase 1 study was designed to determine the maximum tolerated fraction dose (MTFD) of this integrated approach in patients with unresectable LA-ESCC.

sec.title: Study design and ethics
sec.p: This prospective phase 1 study enrolled patients with histologically confirmed ESCC who met the following inclusion criteria: unresectable disease classified as stage T1-4, N0-3, M0-1 according to the 8th edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM staging system, with M1 limited to supraclavicular lymph node metastasis; age between 18 and 80 years; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1; no prior treatment with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery, or immunotherapy for ESCC; no evidence of deep ulceration on baseline esophagoscopy; and adequate hematologic, hepatic, and renal function. Resectability was assessed by a multidisciplinary team (MDT) at baseline for all patients. Sex assigned at birth was recorded at baseline based on medical records. Gender identity was not separately collected.

This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (A2023-005) and is available in the Supplementary Materials. All participants provided written informed consent prior to enrolment. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06020885.

sec.title: Randomisation and masking
sec.p: This phase 1 dose-escalation study did not involve randomisation or masking. Participants were sequentially assigned to predefined radiotherapy dose cohorts according to the protocol. Both investigators and participants were aware of the treatment allocation.

sec.title: Induction chemo-immunotherapy and split-course CCRT
sec.p: Induction chemo-immunotherapy consisted of two cycles of chemo-immunotherapy administered every 21 days, comprising of albumin-bound paclitaxel (260 mg/m2, d1), cisplatin (60 mg/m2, d1), and toripalimab (240 mg, d1).

Tumour response was re-evaluated approximately 2 weeks after completion of two cycles of induction chemo-immunotherapy, followed by a second MDT reassessment of surgical resectability. Patients who remained unresectable proceeded to definitive split-course RT with concurrent oral capecitabine. Split-course RT was delivered in two courses separated by a 4-week break. After the first course of hypo-RT, eligibility for the second RT course required the absence of radiographic or endoscopic disease progression during the planned treatment interval, along with the absence of ≥grade (G) 2 toxicities by the end of this break. After completion of the first course of hypo-RT and a planned 4-week break, patients then underwent comprehensive reassessment, including radiological evaluation of tumour response, endoscopic confirmation of the absence of deep oesophageal ulceration, and cardiopulmonary function assessment. Those meeting predefined safety and efficacy criteria proceeded to a second computed tomography (CT) simulation and radiotherapy planning session, followed by the boost course of conventionally fractionated or moderately hypo-RT. Concurrently, oral capecitabine was administered at a dose of 1000 mg/m2 twice daily on days 1–14 of each radiotherapy course. The schematic diagram of the study design is presented in Fig. 1A.

caption.p: Study design and trial profile. (A) Schematic diagram of the study design: Overview of treatment sequence including induction chemo-immunotherapy followed by split-course RT, with key assessment time points. (B) Trial profile. Abbreviation: RT, radiotherapy.

sec.title: Radiation planning
sec.p: Patients were positioned supine and immobilized using a vacuum cushion to maintain consistent setup. A 4D CT scan with 3-mm slice thickness was performed, covering the region from the cricoid cartilage down to the L2 vertebra. The gross tumour volume (GTV) encompassed the primary tumour and any lymph node involved identified by endoscopy, contrast-enhanced CT, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or positron emission tomography (PET) imaging at baseline. The clinical target volume (CTV) was delineated by expanding the primary GTV by 0.5–1.0 cm laterally and 3.0 cm longitudinally. For nodal GTV, a margin of 0.5 cm laterally and 1.0 cm longitudinally was added to define the CTV. Elective lymph node regions were included according to tumour location: stations 1, 2, and 4 for cervical tumours; stations 1, 2, 4, and 7 for upper thoracic tumours; stations 2, 4, 7, 8, and 9 for middle thoracic tumours; and stations 7, 8, 9, 16, and 17 for lower thoracic tumours. The planning target volume (PTV) was created by adding a uniform 5-mm margin around both the GTV and CTV to compensate for positional variations. For the second course of RT, the GTV was adjusted to reflect tumour regression; however, the cranio-caudal length of the GTV for the primary tumour was kept consistent with that defined at baseline and was not shortened, even in cases of significant tumour shrinkage. The CTV and PTV were then generated using the same expansion margins as in the first course, and elective nodal regions were consistently included. Radiotherapy was delivered using volumetric modulated arc therapy, with daily cone-beam CT imaging for treatment guidance.

Dose planning required that at least 95% of the PTV received the full prescription dose. The maximum dose to any point within the PTV was limited to <110% prescribed dose. Organs at risk (OARs), including the lungs, heart, spinal cord and kidney were contoured accordingly. Dose constraints for the spinal cord were prioritized over target coverage. Detailed OAR dose constraints are provided in Supplementary Table S1.

sec.title: Dose fractionation
sec.p: Split-course RT was delivered in two courses separated by a 4-week break. After the first course of hypo-RT, eligibility for the second RT course required the absence of ≥G2 toxicities by the end of this break. Three dose levels were tested in sequential cohorts of 6 patients (Fig. 1A):

list-item.p: Dose level 1: 30 Gy delivered in 10 daily fractions in the initial course, followed by a boost course of 20 Gy in 10 fractions, with a 4-week interval between courses. The total treatment duration was 8 weeks.

Dose level 2: 28 Gy delivered in 7 daily fractions in the initial course, followed by a boost course of 22 Gy in 10 fractions, with a 4-week interval between courses. The total treatment duration was approximately 7.4 weeks.

Dose level 3: 25 Gy delivered in 5 daily fractions in the initial course, followed by a boost course of 25 Gy in 10 fractions, with a 4-week interval between courses. The total treatment duration was 7 weeks.

sec.title: Treatment response and toxicity evaluation
sec.p: Tumour evaluations were conducted at baseline, 2 weeks after the completion of induction chemo-immunotherapy, 3 weeks following the split-course CCRT, and 2 months after the completion of CCRT. Thereafter, follow-up assessments were scheduled every 3–4 months during the first two years, every 6 months from year 3–5, and annually beyond year 5, until disease progression, initiation of new antitumour therapy, patient withdrawal, or death.

Tumour response was determined using contrast-enhanced CT, MRI and endoscopy, according to a modified version of the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST) version 1.1 that incorporated MRI-based findings.19,20 A clinical complete response (cCR) was defined as the complete disappearance of tumour, mucosal irregularity, or ulceration on endoscopic examination; negative biopsy results from any suspicious lesions; and radiographic resolution of the primary tumour and nodal involvement on T2-weighted MRI (normalization of the oesophageal wall or subtle hypo-intense wall thickening, with no involved nodes, and an apparent diffusion coefficient value of the primary tumour ≥2.64 × 10−3 mm2/s); and no new metastases detected on CT. Partial response (PR) was defined as a complete or partial response based on conventional RECIST criteria, without fulfilling any of the predefined criteria for cCR. Adverse events (AEs), including immune-related adverse events, were prospectively monitored from the initiation of chemo-immunotherapy until 2 months after the completion of split-course CCRT and graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 5.0. Key adverse events of interest, including tracheal/oesophageal fistula, oesophageal stenosis, and pneumonitis, were observed up to one year after completion of CCRT or until the start of new anti-cancer therapy, whichever came first.

To determine the maximum tolerated fraction dose (MTFD) for the combined chemo-immunotherapy and split-course CCRT protocol, all toxicities attributable to radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy were assessed together. Dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) was defined as any treatment-related ≥G3 adverse event, except for G3 hematologic toxicities, any-grade hypersensitivity reactions, and G3 radiation oesophagitis, which were considered expected and clinically manageable toxicities and therefore not dose-limiting.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint of this study was to determine the MTFD. Each dose level was assessed in a cohort of six patients undergoing split-course CCRT at the corresponding radiation dose. The MTFD was defined as the highest dose level at which no more than two patients experienced ≥G3 treatment-related toxicity and no more than one experienced ≥G4 toxicity within 12 months following completion of split-course CCRT. When multiple toxicities occurred in a single patient, only the highest toxicity grade was recorded for analysis. Advancement to the next dose level was allowed if either of the following conditions was met: (a) All six patients had completed CCRT, and at least three had been followed for more than 2 months without experiencing any ≥G3 toxicities. (b) All six patients had been monitored for over 2 months post-CCRT, with no more than two cases of ≥G3 toxicity and no more than one case of ≥G4 toxicity. If neither condition was fulfilled, enrolment at that dose level was discontinued.

The secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), objective response rate (ORR), and the rate of grade 3 or 4 treatment-related toxicities according to CTCAE 5.0. PFS was defined as the interval from study enrolment to the first occurrence of disease progression or death from any cause, or was censored at the date of last follow-up. OS was measured from the date of enrolment until death from any cause or was censored at the last follow-up. ORR was defined as the proportion of patients who achieved a cCR or PR.

Follow-up assessments were performed according to the study protocol. The primary endpoint, MTFD, was evaluated within 12 months. Secondary endpoints included PFS and OS, both assessed up to 1 year; ORR assessed 2 months after completion of CCRT; and the rate of grade 3 or 4 treatment-related toxicities, monitored during the 12-month follow-up period.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics were utilized to summarize patient characteristics. The data-cutoff date was October 31, 2025. Survival rates were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) calculated via the log–log transformation. The ORR and its 95% CI were determined using the Wilson score method, as it provides accurate interval estimates for proportion data in small samples. All statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), GraphPad Prism version 8.0.2, and R software version 4.4.1. No post-hoc analyses or sensitivity analyses were performed. All analyses reported in this study were prespecified. No formal sample size or power calculations were conducted, as the study followed a phase 1 dose-escalation design in which each cohort included six patients.

sec.title: Role of the funding source
sec.p: The funders had no involvement in study design, data collection, data analyses, data interpretation, or the writing of the report.

sec.title: Patient characteristics and treatment disposition
sec.p: Between Aug 31, 2023, and July 23, 2024, 18 patients were enrolled; with equal distribution across the three dose levels (n = 6 per level) (Fig. 1B). Table 1 and Supplementary Table S2 show the baseline characteristics of all patients. The median age was 67 years (interquartile range [IQR], 60–70), with similar age distributions among dose levels. The majority of participants were male (n = 13), and 72.2% (n = 13) had a history of smoking. A history of alcohol use was reported by 7 patients (38.9%). Most patients (77.8%, n = 14) had an ECOG performance status of 0, while the remaining 4 (22.2%) had a status of 1. Tumours were primarily located in the middle (n = 6, 33.3%) and distal (n = 6, 33.3%) oesophagus, followed by the upper (n = 4, 22.2%) and cervical segments (n = 2, 11.2%). Based on clinical TNM classification, 8 patients (44.4%) were diagnosed with stage II-III disease, and 5 (27.8%) had supraclavicular lymph node involvement. The reasons for not undergoing surgical treatment included cervical tumour location (n = 2, 11.1%), T4b disease (n = 2, 11.1%), stage IVB classification (n = 5, 27.8%), surgical contraindication (n = 6, 33.3%) and patient refusal (n = 3, 16.7%).

fn.p: Abbreviations: ECOG PS, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status; IQR, interquartile range; RT, radiotherapy.

sec.p: Seventeen patients underwent induction chemo-immunotherapy according to protocol, whereas one patient received only a single cycle due to treatment refusal. All enrolled patients completed split-course RT and concurrent chemotherapy as planned. No patients received a delayed boost RT beyond the protocol-defined interval. The dosimetric parameters of radiotherapy are summarized in Supplementary Table S3.

sec.title: Primary endpoint and toxicity
sec.p: All treatment-related toxicity occurring within the 12-month follow-up period are summarized in Table 2. All 18 patients were included in the safety analysis. The most frequently observed AEs were lymphopenia (94.4%), esophagitis (88.8%), fatigue (66.6%), and cough (38.9%), with the majority being grade 1 or 2 in severity. G3 toxicities were observed in 13 patients (72.2%), primarily lymphopenia (72.2%) and esophagitis (11.1%). Two patients (11.1%) with G3 esophagitis were both from Dose level 1. None of the patients required nasogastric tube placement or percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy throughout the treatment and follow-up periods. One patient (5.6%) had G2 pneumonitis (Dose level 1). No DLTs, as predefined in the protocol, were observed in any dose group. Consequently, the MTFD was not reached, and dose level 3 was deemed tolerable. Overall, split-course CCRT demonstrated an acceptable safety profile, with manageable toxicities across all dose levels. No treatment-related deaths were reported during the observation period. Immune-related AEs were not observed.

sec.title: Treatment response and survival outcomes
sec.p: Following induction immune-chemotherapy, 2 patients (11.1%) achieved cCR, and 16 patients (88.9%) had PR, yielding an ORR of 100% (Supplementary Table S4). After completion of CCRT, 15 patients (83.3%) achieved cCR and 3 patients (16.7%) maintained PR. The overall post-CCRT cCR rate reached 83.3% (95% CI, 60.8–94.2%) and was consistent across all dose levels (Fig. 2A–B). A typical case of treatment response was demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S1.

caption.p: Tumour responses of patients in each dose levels. (A) Maximum change in tumour size from baseline assessed according to RECIST version 1.1 in study population. The dotted line at −30% represents partial response. (B) Swimmer plot of treatment duration for patients grouped by dose level. Abbreviations: CCRT, concurrent chemoradiotherapy; RECIST, Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours.

sec.p: At a median follow-up of 20.5 months (IQR: 15.4–25.5), 5 patients (27.8%) experienced local progression, all of which were in-field failures (2 in Dose level 1, and 3 in Dose level 2). No regional or distant failures were observed. Median PFS and OS were not reached. The 1-year PFS and OS rates were 88.9% (95% CI, 75.5%–100%) and 94.4% (95% CI, 84.4%–100%), respectively (Fig. 3A–B). The 1-year PFS rate was 83.3% (95% CI, 58.3%–100%), 83.3% (95% CI, 58.3%–100%), and 100% in Dose level 1, Dose level 2, and Dose level 3, respectively. The 1-year OS rate was 83.3% (95% CI, 58.3%–100%), 100%, and 100% in Dose level 1, Dose level 2, and Dose level 3, respectively.

caption.p: Kaplan–Meier survival curves illustrating progression-free survival probability (A) and overall survival probability (B) of the study population. Abbreviation: CI, confidence interval.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this phase 1 trial, we assessed the safety and preliminary efficacy of a dose-escalated split-course RT regimen with concurrent oral capecitabine following induction chemo-immunotherapy in patients with unresectable, LA-ESCC. The regimen proved feasible and well tolerated across all three prespecified dose levels, including the highest schedule of 25 Gy in 5 fractions followed by 25 Gy in 10 fractions. No DLTs were observed during the 12-month safety window, and the MTFD was not reached. All patients completed the planned course of split-course CCRT without treatment discontinuation for toxicity. Early efficacy outcomes were encouraging, with a high rate of cCR and favourable survival, supporting the safety of dose-escalated hypofractionation in this setting and justifying further investigation into this strategy.

Our protocol provides insights into the combination of immunotherapy and CCRT. In the current study, toripalimab with chemotherapy as induction therapy before split-course CCRT represents an innovative approach to reduce tumour burden and stimulate antitumour immunity. In our previous phase 2 study, LA-ESCC patients achieved a cCR rate of 12.1% after two cycles of induction chemo-immunotherapy.10 Following CCRT with 50 Gy in 20 fractions, the cCR rates improved substantially to 67.2% In the present trial, sequential induction chemo-immunotherapy followed by split-course CCRT yielded a cCR rate of 83.3%, substantially higher than the 23.3% reported by Zhang et al. with a median fraction dose of 3 Gy.21 Induction chemo-immunotherapy facilitates significant tumour regression in most patients, thereby enabling reduced target volumes and creating favourable conditions for subsequent fraction-dose-escalated radiotherapy. These findings underscore the potential of this multimodal approach, and further investigation is warranted to optimize combined strategies for maximizing efficacy while maintaining safety.

To harness the therapeutic benefits of hypo-RT while mitigating its toxic effects, we implemented a split-course CCRT protocol featuring an initial hypo-RT phase followed by a planned treatment break. This design allows delivery of a high BED in the first course—beginning with 30 Gy in 10 fractions (dose level 1), a regimen previously established as safe in the palliative ESCC setting,22 and escalating to 25 Gy in 5 fractions (5 Gy/fraction) in dose level 3, an approach supported by analogous hypofractionated regimens in other cancers.15 The subsequent break enables critical mucosal recovery and reassessment of treatment tolerance before initiating a conventional fractionation boost course (2–2.5 Gy per fraction), cumulatively reaching 50 Gy. Although treatment interruptions raise theoretical concerns regarding tumour repopulation, prior evidence has primarily been derived from conventionally fractionated radiotherapy or radiotherapy alone.23,24 In our study, substantial tumour regression was achieved following induction chemo-immunotherapy, and hypo-RT with concurrent chemotherapy was subsequently delivered, which may have mitigated the potential risk of accelerated repopulation. After the break, tumour response was reassessed by imaging and endoscopic evaluation, and continuation to the second course of radiotherapy was permitted only in the absence of disease progression and with acceptable toxicity. This design reflects a deliberate balance between safety optimization and preservation of local disease control. In the current study, this approach yielded encouraging results: after induction therapy, all patients (100%) achieved an objective response (11.1% cCR, 88.9% PR). Following split-course CCRT, the cCR rate rose to 83.3% (95% CI: 60.8–94.2%). Importantly, the initial hypo-RT course contributed to continuous tumour shrinkage and significant mucosal repair during the break, which may have helped reduce the risk of acute ulcerations, massive bleeding, fistula formation, and G3 esophagitis.

Across all three dose levels, no predefined DLTs, G4-5 toxicities, or treatment-related deaths occurred. Only two patients (11.1%) in our trial experienced G3 esophagitis, and no perforation, fistula, or fatal bleeding was observed. Radiation pneumonitis was rare in the current study, with only one case in Dose level 1 experienced G2 pneumonitis and no ≥G3 events. By contrast, reported rates of G3-4 esophagitis in prior hypo-RT series range from 2.8% to 33.3% with fraction sizes of 3.0–6.0 Gy.16,25,26 In conventional fractionated definitive CCRT at standard doses, the incidence of ≥G3 radiation esophagitis, radiation pneumonitis, and oesophageal fistula have been reported to be 7.0%–28.8%, 3%–5%, and 2.5%–10.0%, respectively.5,7,27 Our treatment regimen demonstrated a favourable safety profile. We hypothesize this is due to the pronounced early control of the primary oesophageal tumour, achieved through induction chemoimmunotherapy and the initial course of hypo-RT. The resultant significant tumour shrinkage provided an opportunity for the recovery of oesophageal mucosa, which likely contributed to a lower incidence of fistula formation and massive bleeding. This subsequent mucosal recovery, coupled with improved nutritional status, permitted the administration of a second boost course of conventional CCRT to a total dose of 50 Gy in 2.0–2.5 Gy per fraction. The favourable safety profile of this split-course RT protocol offers a less toxic treatment option for ESCC patients who are elderly or have compromised cardiopulmonary function—populations in which a significant proportion are unable to tolerate standard CCRT and often receive radiotherapy alone or palliative treatment instead.28,29 The pre-boost evaluation further enables individualized adaptation of treatment intensity based on each patient's recovery status. Consequently, this regime not only improves tolerability but also expands treatment eligibility to include patients who would otherwise be deemed unsuitable for standard CCRT.

Beyond its favourable safety profile, the dose-escalated split-course CCRT regimen demonstrated encouraging early efficacy. Several studies have shown that hypo-RT achieves survival outcomes comparable to conventional fractionation.21,30,31 For example, Song et al. reported a median OS of 17 months using definitive CCRT with fraction sizes of 3–6 Gy,16 while our prior trial observed a median OS of 16.4 months with 2.5 Gy per fraction.26 In a retrospective analysis, Jones et al. noted no significant difference in OS or PFS between patients treated with hypo-RT (50–52.5 Gy in 16–20 fractions) and those treated with conventional CCRT (50 Gy in 25 fractions), despite a hazard ratio of 1.73 for OS.30 In the present study, with a median follow-up of 20.5 months, median PFS and OS had not yet been reached, suggest highly favourable efficacy in LA-ESCC. This encouraging anti-tumour activity may be attributed in part to the elevated BED delivered by our protocol. The split-course regimen achieved BED values of 63 Gy, 66.04 Gy, and 68.75 Gy across dose levels, compared to a BED of 60 Gy with conventional 50 Gy in 25 fractions. Furthermore, the hypo-RT regimen may help preserve circulating lymphocyte counts by reducing the number of radiation fractions. In this study, grade 3 lymphopenia, the most common high-grade toxicity, occurred in 72.2% of patients, which compares favorably to the 86% rate reported with conventional fractionation.27 Given that severe lymphopenia has been retrospectively associated with worse overall survival,32 the potential for reduced lympho-toxic effects represents another plausible factor contributing to the promising efficacy observed. Achieving local control for unresectable LA-ESCC while minimizing toxicity remains a critical challenge.

Recent phase 2 studies evaluating induction chemoimmunotherapy followed by conventionally fractionated CCRT have reported encouraging survival outcomes, with 1-year OS rates of approximately 85% and 1-year PFS rates around 70%.10, 11, 12 In our previous study on induction chemo-immunotherapy followed by conventionally fractionated CCRT (50 Gy in 20 fractions), 32.8% of patients had residual disease, which was associated with early local recurrence. In the current study, hypofractionated split-course CCRT resulted in 1-year PFS and OS rates of 88.9% and 94.4%, respectively, with a median follow-up of 20.5 months. Five patients (27.8%) experienced local progression, all of which were in-field failures. Most recurrences occurred in patients with a suboptimal response to induction chemoimmunotherapy and the initial hypo-RT course. Although the current study is limited by a small sample size, a trend suggested that local recurrences were more frequent in the lower dose hypo-RT groups (level 1: 3 Gy per fraction; level 2: 4 Gy per fraction) than in the highest dose group (level 3: 5 Gy per fraction), in which no recurrences were observed. This implies that higher fractional doses, by increasing the BED, may improve tumour control. Although cross-trial comparisons should be interpreted with caution, these data suggest that fraction-dose escalation after tumour shrinkage induced by chemo-immunotherapy may provide additional therapeutic benefit, particularly in terms of local tumour control. The hypofractionated strategy may enhance tumour cell kill and potentially amplify immunogenic effects, thereby optimizing the therapeutic impact of prior immune activation.

Nevertheless, the application of whole course hypo-RT is constrained by a significantly increased risk of severe toxic effects, including high-grade esophagitis and fistula formation. Prior research has established that continuous hypo-RT regimens using fractions ≥3 Gy to total doses >50 Gy are poorly tolerated. For instance, a phase 1/II trial of 3D-conformal hypo-RT for T3–4N0–1M0 ESCC reported reduced tolerability at doses above 5 Gy per fraction and an 8.3% rate of fatal fistula even at 4 Gy per fraction, with the incidence of grade 3 oesophageal toxicity escalating with larger fraction sizes.16 Therefore, a mid-treatment evaluation following the initial hypo-RT course is critical. For patients demonstrating a suboptimal response, which may indicate inherent tumour radio-resistance, this assessment permits the timely discontinuation of the planned boost radiotherapy. This approach avoids the unnecessary toxicity of further radiation and allows for an expedited transition to alternative salvage therapies.

This study has several limitations. The small sample size, consistent with a phase 1 design, limits statistical power to detect rare toxicities and precludes definitive conclusions regarding efficacy. Additionally, comparisons with historical cohorts should be interpreted cautiously, given potential differences in patient characteristics, systemic therapies, radiotherapy techniques, and follow-up duration. A median follow-up of 20.5 months, while sufficient for early safety and efficacy assessment, remains relatively short for evaluating long-term survival outcomes. Moreover, late toxicities associated with hypo-RT, such as fibrosis and oesophageal stenosis, may not yet be fully captured. Longer follow-up is required to comprehensively evaluate long-term safety. Future phase 2 studies are needed to further characterize toxicity and confirm efficacy, and comparative trials with conventional fractionation are warranted to assess the benefits of hypofractionation in combination with immunotherapy. Given the phase 1 design, limited sample size, and primary focus on safety and dose-escalation, formal subgroup analyses were not performed.

In conclusion, in this phase 1 study, fraction dose-escalated split-course CCRT following induction chemo-immunotherapy demonstrated a tolerable safety profile with no MTFD identified at the highest planned dose level. The encouraging early efficacy and manageable toxicity observed in this phase 1 trial support further investigation in larger phase 2/III studies. Integration of immunotherapy with optimized split-course CCRT represents a promising advance in multidisciplinary management for patients with unresectable LA-ESCC.
